result: Children with ADHD exhibited impaired biological motion (BM) perception across all three tasks (local, global, and general) compared to typically developing (TD) children, with significant group differences in accuracy for BM-Local (p=0.003, d=0.71), BM-Global (p<0.001, d=0.85), and BM-General (p<0.001, d=1.09).
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge these group differences as solid findings. The editor states 'children with ADHD were worse at all three BM tasks' and describes these as 'important and solid findings.' Reviewers note the results are 'novel' and 'valuable' with 'sufficient detail' for reproduction, indicating acceptance of the core performance deficits.

result: Local BM processing ability was specifically related to social interaction skills (SRS scores) in children with ADHD. While all three BM tasks correlated negatively with SRS scores across the whole sample, within-group analysis showed this correlation was significant only for the local BM task in the ADHD group (r=-0.461, p=0.004), not the TD group, and not for global or general BM tasks in either group.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly challenge this claim's strength. One reviewer states 'the data are not strong enough to support claims about differences between global and local processing wrt social communication skills' and notes 'the results section shows a correlation between SRS and all three tasks.' Another reviewer emphasizes 'the crucial tests of differences between correlations do not present a clear picture' and that 'many of the differences between correlations are not significant,' attributing this to 'small samples for correlations.'

result: Global BM processing ability significantly improved with age in both ADHD and TD groups. In the ADHD group, age predicted global BM performance (β=0.251, p=0.025) and general BM performance both directly (β=0.365, p<0.001) and indirectly through enhanced global BM processing. Similar age-related improvements were observed in TD children for both global (β=0.396, p=0.017) and general (β=0.330, p=0.049) BM tasks.
evaluation: Reviewers express concern about the theoretical assumptions underlying age-related claims. One reviewer notes 'the authors make some statements about local vs global biological motion processing that may have been made in previous studies, but would appear controversial and not definitive. E.g., that local BM processing does not improve with age.' While the statistical findings are not directly challenged, reviewers indicate 'there are still some elements of the results that need clarification with future work,' suggesting uncertainty about the interpretation of developmental trajectories.

result: General BM perception in children with ADHD was affected by sustained attention, with this relationship mediated by reasoning intelligence (Perceptual Reasoning). Path analysis showed that sustained attention (QbInattention) did not directly predict BM-General performance but was indirectly predicted through Perceptual Reasoning ability. Higher IQ, particularly Perceptual Reasoning (β=0.271, p=0.005), and better global BM processing (β=0.290, p=0.004) predicted better general BM performance.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these findings as part of the study's contributions. The editor summarizes that 'general (local & global combined) BM processing was predicted by age and global BM processing, while reasoning ability mediated the effect of inattention on BM processing.' One reviewer notes the results show 'relationships to indices of social functioning and possible predictors of BM perception (including demographics, reasoning ability and inattention)' without raising concerns about these specific mediation findings.

result: The study included appropriate sample sizes and participant characterization across two experiments. Experiment 1 included 36 TD children and 39 children with ADHD (mean age ~9 years), matched on age but differing in sex distribution. The ADHD group showed higher SRS total scores than TD group (p<0.001). All participants met IQ criteria (>75 for ADHD on WISC-IV; >5th percentile for TD on Raven's matrices).
evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological details without challenge. One reviewer explicitly states 'methods and materials are presented with sufficient detail so the study could be reproduced by independent researchers.' The sample characterization is acknowledged as adequate, though reviewers note 'small samples for correlations' when discussing statistical power for correlation comparisons, which is a separate issue from the basic sample description.

result: The study employed a well-controlled experimental paradigm using point-light displays to separately assess local, global, and general BM processing. The BM-Local task isolated local kinematics by scrambling global configuration; BM-Global isolated global configuration by equating local kinematics between conditions; and BM-General allowed use of both cue types. Tasks were presented in fixed order to maintain participant naivety.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse the experimental design. One reviewer states 'they use a task that appears well controlled' and describes the paradigm as 'innovative, albeit not novel.' The editor notes the study uses 'point light displays to measure biological motion (BM) perception' without raising methodological concerns. The task design is treated as a strength enabling the dissociation of local and global processing mechanisms.

result: In the ADHD group, the ability to process global BM cues was positively correlated with performance in processing general BM cues (β=0.290, p=0.004), whereas no such correlation was found in the TD group. This suggests children with ADHD may rely more on global BM cues when both local and global cues are available, while TD children can extract and integrate both cue types.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding as part of the study's contribution to understanding processing mechanisms. One reviewer notes the authors 'raise some interesting mechanistic possibilities for differences in local and global motion processing, which are distinctions worth exploring.' While reviewers express concerns about other correlation comparisons, this specific finding about differential reliance on global cues in the ADHD group is not directly challenged and is treated as contributing to mechanistic understanding.

result: The study employed validated assessment instruments with established psychometric properties, including the Chinese versions of K-SADS-PL-C DSM-5, ADHD Rating Scale, Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS), and QB test for measuring diagnostic status, symptom severity, social functioning, and sustained attention.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the validity or appropriateness of the assessment instruments. One reviewer explicitly states 'methods and materials are presented with sufficient detail so the study could be reproduced,' implicitly accepting the measurement tools as appropriate. The psychometric properties of these instruments are not questioned in any review.
